title: Stresses on soil and seepage
summary: One idea dominates this subchapter and explains most of the questions: only the effective stress, σ′ = σ − u, controls strength and volume change. Once that is held, quick sand, piping, the effect of a rising water table and the whole of consolidation theory follow as consequences rather than separate facts. The remaining material is Darcy's law and its applications — flow nets, permeability tests, and the two creep theories for seepage under a hydraulic structure.

sections.heading: Effective stress — the governing principle
sections.body:
**Terzaghi's principle of effective stress:**

> **σ′ = σ − u**

where σ is the **total** stress, u the **pore water pressure**, and σ′ the **effective** stress carried by the soil skeleton through grain-to-grain contact.

**Only the effective stress controls shear strength and volume change.** Total stress does not, and pore pressure alone does not. Every important consequence in soil mechanics follows from this:

| Change | Effect on σ′ | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Water table rises** | u rises, σ′ **falls** | **Strength falls** — the mechanism of most rain-triggered slope failures |
| Water table falls (pumping) | u falls, σ′ **rises** | **Settlement** — the cause of regional subsidence from over-pumping |
| Load applied to saturated clay | u rises first, σ′ unchanged | No immediate strength gain; **consolidation** follows as u dissipates |
| **Upward seepage** | u rises | σ′ → 0 gives **quick sand** |
| Submergence | Both rise equally | σ′ **unchanged** — a subtle and frequently examined point |

That last row deserves attention. Adding water **above** the ground surface increases both σ and u by the same amount, so **σ′ does not change** and the soil neither strengthens nor settles. It is why a flooded site does not itself consolidate.

**Computing the profile.** Total stress is the weight of everything above, including water:

> **σ = Σ(γ · thickness)**, using **γ_sat below the water table**
> **u = γ_w · h_w**
> **σ′ = σ − u**, or directly **σ′ = Σ(γ′ · thickness)** below the water table with **γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w**

The second route is quicker, and the fact that it works is itself a check on the arithmetic.

**Capillary rise** creates **negative** pore pressure (suction) above the water table, so σ′ is **increased** there. That apparent cohesion is what lets a damp sand stand in a vertical cut — and why the cut collapses when it dries out or is flooded.

**Stress increase from applied load.** **Boussinesq's** solution for a point load on a semi-infinite elastic half space:

> **σ_z = (3Q/2πz²) · [1/(1 + (r/z)²)]^{5/2}**

The practical outcomes matter more than the formula: stress **decreases with depth roughly as 1/z²**, and the **pressure bulb (isobar)** of 20% of the applied pressure extends to about **1.5 to 2 times the width** of the loaded area. That is why the depth of soil exploration is specified as 1.5–2 B — below it the added stress is too small to cause appreciable settlement.

**Westergaard's** solution assumes a layered soil with rigid horizontal reinforcement and gives **lower** stresses at depth than Boussinesq — more realistic for stratified deposits. The **2:1 approximate method** simply spreads the load over an area widening at 2 vertical to 1 horizontal, and is adequate for many settlement estimates.

**Newmark's influence chart** handles a loaded area of **any shape**, by counting the influence areas covered by the plan drawn to scale.

sections.heading: Permeability and Darcy's law
sections.body:
> **v = k · i**,  where **i = h/L** is the hydraulic gradient

valid only for **laminar** flow, which covers virtually all natural seepage except through very coarse gravel and rockfill.

**Two velocities**, and confusing them is a standard error:

| Velocity | Expression | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Discharge velocity v** | k·i | Over the **gross** area — a fictitious average |
| **Seepage velocity v_s** | **v/n** | The **actual** velocity through the voids — always **larger** |

Water can only flow through the voids, so the real velocity must exceed the nominal one by the reciprocal of the porosity.

**Typical permeabilities**, spanning **ten orders of magnitude** — which is why soil type matters so much more here than anywhere else:

| Soil | k (m/s) |
|---|---|
| Clean gravel | 10⁻¹ – 10⁻² |
| Clean sand | 10⁻² – 10⁻⁵ |
| Silty sand, silt | 10⁻⁵ – 10⁻⁸ |
| **Clay** | **< 10⁻⁹** |

**Factors affecting k:** **grain size** (k ∝ D_10², Allen Hazen), **void ratio**, **soil structure**, **degree of saturation**, **viscosity of the fluid** (hence temperature), and the presence of **stratification**.

**Stratified soils are strongly anisotropic**, and the two averages are quite different:

> **Parallel (horizontal) flow: k_H = Σ(k_i H_i)/ΣH_i** — an **arithmetic** mean, dominated by the **most permeable** layer
> **Perpendicular (vertical) flow: k_V = ΣH_i / Σ(H_i/k_i)** — a **harmonic** mean, dominated by the **least permeable** layer

So **k_H is always greater than k_V**, typically by a factor of 2 to 10 in natural deposits. The reason is intuitive: in parallel flow the water uses the easy layer, while in series flow it is held up by the tight one — exactly like resistances in an electrical circuit.

**Measurement:**

| Test | Suits | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Constant head** | **Coarse** soils | Flow is fast enough to measure a steady discharge |
| **Falling head** | **Fine** soils | Flow too slow for that; the fall of head in a standpipe is measured |
| **Pumping out** (field) | Any, over a large mass | Gives a **mass average**, which is what actually governs seepage |
| Consolidation test | Clays | k derived from c_v and m_v |

The **field** value is the one that matters for a dewatering or seepage problem, because laboratory specimens omit the fissures and laminations that dominate real flow.

sections.heading: Flow nets and seepage quantity
sections.body:
A **flow net** is a graphical solution of Laplace's equation for two-dimensional steady seepage, drawn as two families of curves:

| Family | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Flow lines** | Paths followed by water particles |
| **Equipotential lines** | Lines of equal **total head** |

**Properties, each with a reason:**

- Flow lines and equipotential lines **cross at right angles** — because flow is normal to lines of equal potential.
- The fields formed are **approximately squares** (curvilinear).
- **No two flow lines cross**, and no two equipotential lines cross.
- The **discharge between adjacent flow lines is equal**, so where the flow channel narrows the **velocity and gradient increase**.
- The **head drop between adjacent equipotential lines is equal**.

> **q = k · H · (N_f / N_d)**

with **N_f** the number of **flow channels** and **N_d** the number of **equipotential drops**. Note that N_f and N_d are counts of *spaces*, not of lines.

**Uses of a flow net:** seepage quantity, **pore pressure at any point**, the **exit gradient** (hence piping safety), and the **uplift pressure** on a structure's base.

**Boundary conditions** determine the net: the upstream and downstream ground surfaces are **equipotentials**, an impervious boundary (the base of a sheet pile, a clay stratum) is a **flow line**, and in an earth dam the **top flow line (phreatic line)** is a free surface at atmospheric pressure, approximated by **Casagrande's parabola**.

**Quick sand** is a **condition, not a type of soil** — the point of the standard question. It occurs where **upward seepage force exactly cancels the effective stress**:

> **σ′ = 0** when **i = i_c = (G − 1)/(1 + e) ≈ 1** for most soils

At that gradient the soil has **no shear strength at all**, since strength depends on σ′. Any soil can be brought to this condition; fine sands and silts are simply the ones in which it is commonly encountered.

**Piping (internal erosion)** is the progressive **backward erosion** of soil by seepage beneath a hydraulic structure. It begins at the downstream exit, where the gradient is highest, and works upstream along a pipe until the structure is undermined. Guarded against by:

| Measure | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Lengthening the seepage path** — cut-offs, sheet piles, upstream apron | Reduces the exit gradient |
| **Inverted filter** with a launching apron at the exit | Allows water out but holds soil in |
| **Increasing the weight** of the downstream floor | Resists uplift |
| **Relief wells / drains** | Reduce pore pressure |

**The two creep theories** examined for weirs and barrages:

| Theory | Assumption |
|---|---|
| **Bligh's creep** | Creep length = **sum of horizontal and vertical paths**, all equally effective |
| **Lane's weighted creep** | **Horizontal** paths weighted at **⅓** of vertical |

Both were superseded by **Khosla's theory of independent variables**, which used **potential flow theory** to show that what matters is the **exit gradient** and the **outer faces of the end sheet piles** — not the total creep length — and that **intermediate sheet piles are largely ineffective**. Safe exit gradients: **1/5–1/6 shingle**, **1/6–1/7 coarse sand**, **1/7 fine sand**.

sections.heading: Consolidation
sections.body:
**Consolidation** is the **time-dependent reduction in volume of a saturated soil under sustained load, caused by the expulsion of pore water.** It applies above all to **clay**, because in sand the water escapes almost instantly and settlement is effectively immediate.

**The mechanism, in three stages:**

1. Load applied → the **pore water takes it all**, so **u rises by Δσ** and **σ′ is unchanged**. No strength gain, no settlement yet.
2. Water begins to drain out → **u falls, σ′ rises**, and the soil compresses.
3. When u has returned to its original value, **σ′ has risen by the full Δσ** and primary consolidation is complete.

So consolidation is the **transfer of load from the water to the soil skeleton** over time. That single sentence explains why it is slow (water must physically flow out through a low-permeability material) and why it stops (there is no more excess pressure to dissipate).

**The oedometer (consolidometer) test** loads a laterally confined specimen in increments, each held until settlement ceases, giving the **e – log σ′** curve:

| Parameter | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Compression index C_c** | Slope of the **virgin** portion of the e – log σ′ curve |
| Recompression index C_r | Slope of the reloading curve — much flatter |
| **Coefficient of compressibility a_v** | −de/dσ′ |
| **Coefficient of volume change m_v** | a_v/(1 + e_0) |
| **Coefficient of consolidation c_v** | k/(m_v γ_w) — governs the **rate** |

**Skempton's correlation: C_c = 0.009 (LL − 10)** for remoulded normally consolidated clay — a useful check when no test result is available.

**Settlement:**

> **S_c = (C_c H / (1 + e_0)) · log₁₀[(σ′_0 + Δσ)/σ′_0]**

Note the **logarithm**: doubling the stress increase does **not** double the settlement, and a given increment causes much less settlement at depth (where σ′_0 is already large) than near the surface.

**Preconsolidation and OCR.**

> **OCR = preconsolidation pressure σ′_c / present effective overburden σ′_0**

| OCR | State | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| **= 1** | **Normally consolidated** | Follows the virgin curve; settles substantially |
| **> 1** | **Over-consolidated** | Follows the flat recompression curve; settles **far less** until σ′_c is exceeded |
| < 1 | Under-consolidated | Still consolidating under its own weight |

A clay is over-consolidated because it **carried a greater load in the past** — since eroded overburden, a melted ice sheet, a demolished building, or desiccation. **Casagrande's construction** on the e – log σ′ curve locates σ′_c. Recognising an over-consolidated clay is worth a great deal in practice, because the settlement estimate can fall by an order of magnitude.

**Rate of consolidation — Terzaghi's theory:**

> **T_v = c_v t / d²**

where **d is the length of the drainage path**. T_v = **0.197 at U = 50%** and **0.848 at U = 90%**.

**Time varies as the SQUARE of the drainage path**, which is the most useful practical consequence: a clay layer draining **both** ways has d = H/2 and consolidates **four times faster** than the same layer draining one way. It is also why **sand drains and prefabricated vertical drains** work — they do not change how much settlement occurs, only how fast, by shortening the drainage path radially from metres to centimetres.

**Secondary compression** continues after primary consolidation is complete, at constant effective stress, from creep of the soil structure. It is significant in **organic and highly plastic** soils and is quantified by the coefficient **C_α** against **log time**.

**Total settlement = immediate (elastic) + primary consolidation + secondary compression.** In **sand** it is essentially all immediate; in **clay** primary consolidation dominates and takes years. Knowing which applies decides the whole analysis.

formulas.label: Effective stress
formulas.note: Only σ′ controls strength and volume change. Submergence raises σ and u equally, leaving σ′ unchanged.

formulas.label: Darcy's law and seepage velocity
formulas.expression: v = k i ;   v_s = v / n
formulas.note: Laminar flow only. Seepage velocity is always larger than discharge velocity.

formulas.label: Equivalent permeability of a stratified soil
formulas.expression: k_H = Σ(k_i H_i)/ΣH_i  (arithmetic) ;   k_V = ΣH_i / Σ(H_i/k_i)  (harmonic)
formulas.note: k_H > k_V always. Parallel flow uses the easy layer; series flow is held up by the tight one.

formulas.label: Seepage from a flow net
formulas.note: N_f flow channels, N_d equipotential drops — counts of spaces, not lines.

formulas.label: Critical hydraulic gradient (quick sand)
formulas.note: At i_c the upward seepage force cancels σ′, so the soil has no shear strength.

formulas.label: Consolidation settlement
formulas.note: Logarithmic, so the same stress increment causes less settlement at depth. C_c ≈ 0.009(LL − 10).

formulas.label: Time factor
formulas.note: Time varies as the SQUARE of the drainage path. Double drainage is four times faster.

formulas.label: Boussinesq stress increase (point load)
formulas.note: Stress falls roughly as 1/z². The 20% isobar reaches about 1.5–2 times the loaded width.

formulas.label: Over-consolidation ratio
formulas.note: OCR = 1 normally consolidated, > 1 over-consolidated (settles far less). Casagrande's construction gives σ′_c.
